theme: The Beatitudes; salt and light; the law fulfilled
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 5:1-20. This is the opening of the Sermon on the Mount. Read the Beatitudes slowly, one at a time, and notice how each begins with a blessing and ends with a promise.
settingTheScene: Jesus goes up on a mountain, sits down as a teacher would, and speaks to his disciples while crowds listen. Matthew has just shown Jesus as the new Israel. Now he shows him as the new Moses, giving a teaching from a mountain, as Moses did at Sinai. The Sermon is not a list of requirements for earning God’s favor. It is a portrait of life in the kingdom that has arrived, addressed to people who already belong to him.
observation: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (5:3).
“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (5:4).
“Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (5:5).
“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (5:6).
“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (5:8).
“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness” sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ (5:10).
“You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden” (5:14).
“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (5:17).
interpretation:
The Beatitudes turn the world’s idea of success upside down. The people called blessed are the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, and the persecuted. These are not the ones the world admires. Yet each is promised something: the kingdom, comfort, the earth, satisfaction, mercy, the sight of God. The blessing is not a reward for being good enough. These are people who know their need, and the kingdom belongs to those who know they cannot get there on their own.

The first and last Beatitudes promise the same thing, the kingdom of heaven, which frames the whole list. The ones between them describe what kingdom people are like: they grieve over sin, they are gentle, they long for what is right, they show mercy, they have undivided hearts, and they make peace. And as the verses go on, Jesus tells them to expect opposition.

He then calls his followers salt and light. Salt preserves and flavors, and light shows the way. Both are useless if hidden or diluted. The point is not to draw attention to ourselves but that people “may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.”

Verses 17 to 20 are the hinge. Jesus did not come to throw away the Old Testament. He came to fulfill it, which means to bring it to its intended goal. The law and prophets pointed to him, and he completes what they began. And when he says that our righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, he sets up an impossible standard that only he can meet and then give to us. The rest of the Sermon shows how deep that righteousness goes.
connection: Exodus 19 and 20 describe the giving of the law from a mountain. Isaiah 61:1-3 promises good news for the poor and comfort for those who mourn. Psalm 37:11 says the meek shall inherit the land. Psalm 24:3-4 asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD, and the answer is the clean of hands and pure of heart. Philippians 2:15 says believers shine as lights in the world. Romans 10:4 says Christ is the end, or goal, of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
application:
Pick one Beatitude and ask where it describes you or challenges you. Pray about that specific one today.

Ask what “poor in spirit” would look like in your work, your marriage, or your church. How would you act if you knew you needed God for everything?

Do one visible good work today that points toward the Father, not toward you.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to make you poor in spirit, aware of your need.
Tell him what you hunger and thirst for.
Ask him to let your light shine so that others give glory to him.
